1:
The title sets the whole chapter arguing. Keil and Delitzsch take the prefixed letter as it is always taken at the head of a psalm, as marking authorship, and so make Solomon the author against the subscription that closes the psalm; they support it from style, finding not the least kinship with the psalms of David but rather the proverb-like distichs with their artificial and almost sluggish manner, the wide geographic range, the richness of figures drawn from nature, and the points of contact with the Book of Job. John Calvin reaches the opposite conclusion from the same inscription, which he thinks settles nothing; since the close calls it the last of David’s prayers he judges David the author, and adds that Solomon could not without vanity have predicted the glory of his own reign. His own conjecture is that Solomon reduced his father’s dying prayers into poetical measure so that they might be kept in remembrance. Adam Clarke lays out the versions — the Chaldee saying by the hand of Solomon, spoken prophetically, the Syriac calling it a psalm of David when he had constituted Solomon king, the rest attributing it to Solomon — and settles on David in his last days.

How far the psalm reaches beyond Solomon divides them more sharply. Augustine of Hippo holds that things are spoken here which could not apply to that Solomon at all, so that the very name is figurative, since it means peace-maker and belongs most truly to the Mediator through whom enemies are reconciled. Matthew Henry reasons from the same impossibility: the kingdom here is to last as long as the sun, while Solomon’s was soon extinct, and before the end of his reign there were both trouble and unrighteousness, so that even the Jewish expositors understand it of the Messiah. John Gill simply names the king as Christ and reports that the old synagogue read it so. C.H. Spurgeon makes the double reference structural, since Solomon was both king and king’s son and so is our Lord, and looks for the day when the warring type is displaced by the prince of peace. John Calvin alone puts a brake on it: those who interpret the psalm simply as a prophecy of the kingdom of Christ seem to him to put a construction on the words that does violence to them, and he warns against giving opponents occasion to cry out that we apply to Christ, sophistically, things which do not directly refer to him.

The mountains that bring peace produce the sharpest textual quarrel. Adam Clarke asks what the little hills by righteousness can mean, answers that it has no meaning, and says the reason is that the verse has been falsely divided: the words in righteousness belong at the head of the next verse, and the old Greek version has the true division. Charles Ellicott keeps the clause where it stands but changes its mood, rendering it as a wish that the mountains and hills bring forth peace to the people in righteousness, and noting that the verb properly means to lift up and is used elsewhere of bearing fruit, peace being the natural fruit of righteousness; he adds that the hills are the characteristic feature of a land which is not merely mountainous but a heap of mountains. John Gill gathers older readings instead: the nations and their kings, comparable to mountains; or the sheer abundance of fruit, so that no one would contend about gathering it but each would invite his neighbour; or simply the inhabitants of the mountains. John Wesley, noting that judgments stands in the plural because the one office had many branches, thinks of the mountains as the dangerous places, haunted by robbers and wild beasts, so that peace there implies peace everywhere; Charles Ellicott observes that the article is wanting before both king and king’s son.
5:
Who is feared here nobody can quite settle. Charles Ellicott renders the clause literally as a wish that they fear Thee coevally with the sun and in the face of the moon, sets beside it a Latin line promising that Aratus shall endure as long as sun and moon, and then declines the question: whether God or the king is the object of the fear must remain unanswered. John Wesley answers it without hesitation for God, and takes the verse to mean that true religion shall be established along with peace. John Gill allows either the oppressors themselves or, rather, the people of God fearing the Messiah. Adam Clarke, who had placed the psalm firmly in David’s last days, here goes furthest of all: there is no sense in which this can be spoken of Solomon, nor indeed of any other man, and it belongs to Christ alone. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the idiom, explaining the two phrases as periphrases for unlimited time, the one meaning during the whole duration of the sun and the other so long as the moon shines.

The rain on the mown grass turns on one word. Charles Ellicott says it means a shearing, used elsewhere of a fleece and of a hay crop, so that the picture is either a mown field on which a shower brings fresh growth or meadow grass still standing ready to be cut. John Gill collects the same range and more, the shorn fleece of the old versions, the grass shorn by locusts of the Targum, and grass shorn by sheep, which classical writers describe as shearing it by biting; he also hears the dew on the fleece behind the figure. Adam Clarke prefers pastured land, and reads the whole image from the night dew that restores by darkness what the cattle have eaten by day, quoting for it the most accomplished of all poets and agriculturists in Dryden’s version, and then giving the plain prose because poetry, he says, always says too much or too little. John Wesley takes the rain for the doctrine brought down from heaven.

The dominion from sea to sea is measured differently by each. Adam Clarke makes it exact and historical: the Euphrates on the east, the Philistines on the western sea, Egypt to the south, so that Solomon held as tributaries the kingdoms lying between and possessed all the land covenanted to Abraham; but as the words may refer to Christ, everything may be taken in its utmost latitude. John Gill denies the fit altogether, since Solomon’s rule reached only to the border of Egypt. John Wesley keeps both, naming the river as the border of Canaan allotted by God but enjoyed only by David, Solomon and Christ. Charles Ellicott weighs the question openly, noting that the original is more poetical and would give tread down the nations from sea to sea, and that the vague ends of the earth and the hyperbolic phrases of the surrounding verses favour a merely poetical reading, though the named places of the following verse pull the other way. C.H. Spurgeon takes it as wide as it will go, from one ocean to the other, and adds that men speak of the emperor of all the Russias but that his King shall rule all mankind — while leaving to others the question whether that reign comes before or after the personal advent. John Gill reads the flourishing of the righteous under the figure of the palm, which grows the more the more it is pressed.
9:
Who the wilderness dwellers are is unsettled from the versions onward. John Gill reports that the old Greek and others render the word Ethiopians, as of people living in a dry land parched by the sun, and takes that for a prophecy of their conversion; he notes too that the same word is used of the wild beasts of the field, to which wicked men may be compared, and that one Jewish commentator keeps it to the inhabitants of the desert, instancing the tribes of the Arabian wastes and, more generally, the Gentiles. Adam Clarke lists the versions that give Ethiopians and the one that gives islands, and prefers a third sense, of those who live by the sea-coasts and support themselves by navigation and fishing. Charles Ellicott takes them for the nomad tribes wandering over the desert, while granting that the word elsewhere means wild animals. Keil and Delitzsch settle the ambiguity by rule: the word serves for both the animals and the men of the desert and must be determined each time by its context, and here they are men beyond all dispute. Of the licking of the dust Charles Ellicott says only that it alludes to the eastern etiquette of prostration before a sovereign, where Adam Clarke reads a subjugation so complete that the conquered become proselytes.

Whether the gifts are tribute is the sharpest disagreement in the entry. Charles Ellicott renders the phrase literally as return presents and insists it does not mean an interchange of royal gifts but the payment of tribute, illustrating it by our own words revenue and custom-house returns. Adam Clarke denies exactly that: the word signifies a grateful or friendly offering, and Solomon did not reign over the province whose capital was Tarsus, nor had he any jurisdiction in the country from which the queen came who brought him such great gifts; the second word used here, he adds, means a compensative present made on account of benefits received, and Solomon gave presents in return. John Gill leaves the place itself open between the sea, so that the kings meant are those of its islands, and a large country inhabited by the Celtae, distinct from the islands. Charles Ellicott thinks the mention of the isles favours identifying the name with the Tartessus of the Greeks, and divides the two remaining names between the continents, the Joktanic kingdom covering most of Yemen and so standing for Arabia, and the Cushite one standing for Africa. John Wesley keeps to remote countries reached by sea.

On the homage of all kings John Gill insists the worship is religious and not civil, since it is due to one who is God equal with the Father, and applies it both to the kings of the earth in the latter day and to those made kings by grace. Adam Clarke holds the historical line and lets it break: the verses are fully explained by the account of the wisdom and riches that drew every man to bring his present year by year, and if the expressions are taken to mean literally all the habitable globe they cannot be applied to Solomon at all, though when the whole earth receives the gospel they may be applied to Christ. John Wesley says flatly that this could not be said of Solomon with any truth or colour. Charles Ellicott only changes the mood again, reading let all kings rather than they shall.
12:
Two of them read these verses as the ground of everything asked before. Keil and Delitzsch call the elevation of the king to the dominion of the world the reward of his condescension, since he shows himself the helper and protecting lord of the poor and oppressed, who are the especial object on which God’s eye is set, and their blood is precious in his eyes. Charles Ellicott reaches the same point from the grammar, insisting the verb here must be present, for he delivereth, so that the wide sway is asked on the strength of a justice already shown; and both of them notice, independently, that the verse is almost word for word what stands in the book of Job. C.H. Spurgeon makes the same connection devotionally: men submit not because they dread an overwhelming power but because they are won by a just and condescending rule.

The crying of the needy draws out C.H. Spurgeon further than the rest. The King permits them to be so needy as to be driven to cry bitterly, and then hears them; a cry is the native language of a needy soul, done with fine phrases and long orations; and against the proverb that God helps those who help themselves he sets the truer word, that his King helps those who cannot help themselves nor find help in others — let them look to him, for he is looking for them. He adds that the rod of correction falls lightly, the King being sparing of rebukes and not sparing in consolations. John Gill defines the needy as those who are not only in want but sensible of it.

What the deceit and the violence are divides them along the usual line. Adam Clarke keeps both in the courts: because the poor are uneducated they are liable to be deceived and because they are helpless they are liable to oppression, so that under this king no man shall suffer because he was deceived, though the letter of the law be against him; and if blood has been spilt he shall seek it out and visit it on the murderer though he were the chief in the land and of the blood royal. John Wesley calls them the two ways by which the lives of men are usually destroyed, and makes the king a true father who will not be prodigal of his subjects’ lives but will severely avenge their blood. John Gill turns both inward, reading deliverance from the deceitfulness of sin, from the old serpent and from false teachers who would deceive the very elect if they could, and from the violence of sin’s dominion and of the strong man armed. Charles Ellicott says only that the parallelism settles the sense, the life of his people being dear to the king, who therefore protects them from violence.
15:
Who prays, and for whom, is disputed three ways. Charles Ellicott holds that the subject can only be the man whose protection from fraud and violence was described in the verse before: he will live, and will bring his benefactor rich gifts and daily blessing; and the rendering that makes prayer offered to the king he calls quite inadmissible. Adam Clarke reads it politically, from the two marks by which conquered countries showed their subjection — their money stamped with the conqueror’s name, and a duty to pray for him in acts of public worship — adding that this king will not act as conquerors generally do but will give the conquered the same laws and privileges as his own subjects, and so be daily praised. C.H. Spurgeon takes the prayer as made for his King, which he calls a very sweet idea, and grounds it thus: the church is his body and the truth his sceptre, so that in pleading for these we pray for him; though he allows that the words may also be read as through him. Charles Ellicott supports the gold by an old historian’s admiring account of the quantity used in adorning houses in that country, wealth probably acquired by commerce with India.

The next verse is a handful or an abundance, and nothing between. Charles Ellicott derives the word from a root meaning to spread and renders it abundance, rearranging the clauses to read that there be abundance of corn on the earth and that on the mountain tops it wave like the cedars; the verb rendered wave, he adds, is used elsewhere of earthquakes and violent storm, suggesting not the quiet motion of a sunny cornfield but as if the mountains themselves were under cultivation and their crowning woods were suddenly turned to grain, while the older versions’ picture of lowland corn overtopping Lebanon he calls grotesque. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same word independently, noting that the term occurs only here and is correctly derived by the Jewish lexicographers from a root meaning to extend or expand, so that it signifies abundance. John Wesley builds the opposite case on the opposite reading: a handful intimates the small beginnings of the kingdom, and therefore does not agree to Solomon, whose kingdom was as large at the beginning of his reign as at the end, but agrees exactly to Christ. John Gill reads it the same way, of one made little account of here and of a kingdom that came without observation. Adam Clarke keeps the handful but makes it agricultural, a handful sown on a mountain top growing strong, and admits that many puzzling criticisms have been raised on the verse and that he gives only what he believes to be the sense.

On the enduring name Adam Clarke claims a literal fulfilment already, since the king is celebrated east and west and his writings still remain, and then states his method outright: he knows these things are thought to belong properly to Christ, and in reference to him they are all true and more, but he believes them properly applicable to Solomon, since it is the business of a commentator to find out the literal sense and the historical fact and not to seek allegories and mysteries where there is no certain evidence of them — while where the writers of the New Testament quote and apply such passages, we not only may but should follow them. John Gill reads the endurance as an office rather than a fame, since even a tyrant’s fame may last, and notes that this king will have no successor. Charles Ellicott prefers have issue for the second clause, literally send out new shoots, allows bless themselves in him for the third, and sets beside the whole a dedication wishing a ruler long life and children who will say that she wrought her people lasting good.
18:
The doxology is taken as settled ground by most and as an occasion for a warning by one. Matthew Henry makes the thanksgiving itself the point: so sure is every word of God that we have reason to give thanks for what he has said though it be not yet done; and he notes that it is only in God’s name that we can contribute anything to his glory, while that name is itself exalted above all blessing and praise. Keil and Delitzsch observe that this closing blessing is more full-toned than the one ending the first book, and that God is here called by the covenant name deliberately, because the book just ending contains none but psalms that avoid it, the last clause being borrowed from the wilderness narrative. John Gill reads the glorious name as every name belonging to this King, like ointment poured forth. C.H. Spurgeon declines to expound at all, quoting an older writer to the effect that these verses explain themselves and call rather for profound gratitude and emotion of heart than for an exercise of the understanding, being meant for adoration and not for exposition.

Adam Clarke uses the same verses for two arguments nobody else attempts. The first is a syllogism: God alone works miracles, so that wherever there is a miracle there is God; Christ most incontrovertibly wrought such miracles; therefore Christ is God. The second is a remark on what the father was not shown. He foresaw all the grandeur and equity of his son’s reign, but God did not reveal to him the apostasy of that beloved son, nor that the wise and prosperous man would debase the divine worship and establish the grossest idolatry; this was hidden from his eyes so that his heart might not be grieved and he might die in peace. And besides, Clarke adds, there was still much contingency in the business, for God would not predict as absolutely certain a thing still poised between a possibility of being and not being, the scale of which he had left, as he leaves all contingencies, to the free will of his creature to turn.

The closing line about the prayers being ended is read as biography by three and as bibliography by one. John Wesley takes it plainly, that this was the last psalm David composed, written a little before his death. Adam Clarke agrees and adds that pieces of his found later in the book have got out of their proper connection. John Gill offers two accounts, that this was the last he wrote, or that it was the last of those he himself put together and digested in order, the remainder being collected afterwards by other hands. Keil and Delitzsch treat the line as evidence about the making of the book: it is the superscription of the primary collection and not part of the doxology, which has only been inserted between the two; a parallel stands at the close of the controversial speeches in the book of Job; and since no one surveying the whole Psalter, with the many psalms of David that follow, could possibly have set this keystone here, the line must be older than the division into five books, which makes it a significant indication about how the collection arose. C.H. Spurgeon reads it as an abdication: the writer strips himself of his own royalty and becomes only the son of Jesse, content to subside into nothing before the crowned King, and asks what more he could possibly have to ask.
